Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Fairbairn
Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
This will be my last President’s Column. My 2nd
term is up and a new GVWG president will be
elected at our AGM in a few days. During my 4
years as president, I’ve had the opportunity and
honour to work with and develop friendships with
quite a few amazing people. These are the people
on the board and the volunteers behind the
scenes who work collectively, and seemingly tirelessly, to ensure the GVWG runs smoothly and
continues to provide value, education, and entertainment to our members. These are the people
who have been responsible for keeping the
GVWG alive and, amazingly, thriving during these
past two difficult pandemic years.
In fact, it was two years ago this month during our
2020 AGM that we had our last in person meeting
before going into lockdown. Little did I know
when I accepted that second term as president
what challenges were in store for us only a few
short weeks later. Over the past two years,
thanks to the above-mentioned group of volunteers, the club has, out of necessity, reinvented
itself. This has been no small feat by any means,
and I simply do not have the words to properly
acknowledge and thank everyone who has been
involved in this journey. You all know who you
are and you all rock!
You’re not quite rid of me yet, though. I may not
be writing this column every month and you
won’t see my face chairing our monthly meetings,
but I’ll still be putting out this newsletter every
month and you’ll still have to put up with me in
the Editor’s Notes.
Signing off…
Steve
Lots of great articles this month. Steve Hansen is
back with his safety column regarding learning to
turn on YouTube.
Bruce talks about the inspiration for his demonstration of turning 3-Cornered Boxes at this
month’s GVWG meeting and Gary Burns tells us
about his initial adventures into resin casting and
wood stabilization.
John Hammond explains how his magnetic dust
hose system works and includes plans for you to
build your own.
Sheila continues her monthly column documenting her journey as a new turner. As usual,
there are lots of great tips in the Tech Talk article
that recaps the January live Tech Talk meeting.
Please keep those articles coming! Send your articles, tips, etc. to editor@gvwg.ca. For inclusion in
the next newsletter, please try to have them submitted to me at least 5 days before our monthly
meeting.
As always, all feed back is welcomed and valued.
Steve

Page 4
Like a lot of my projects, the bowl full of napkin
rings came about due to a combination of loosely
connected events, starting with the Presidents
Challenge to make rings.
I acquired the Holly wood from a client who commission me to make a Water Jug stand. The client
had acquired the Holly wood from a friend and
wanted to have the Water Jug stand turned from
it. However, the round of wood was not dried correctly and it had several cracks making it unusable
for the stand project.
The client gave me the Holly wood to burn it in my
shop wood stove. I actually had not looked that
closely at the wood and thought it was Maple.
When I started cutting up the round with my chainsaw, I realized it was Holly and decided to see if I
could salvage anything from the cracked wood.
After cutting out a couple of small bowl blanks, I
realized I could make up a bunch of napkin rings
from the bits and pieces.
I have never turned napkin rings before, so I was
tempted to go to Youtube to see how napkin rings
are turned, but instead I decided to just figure it
out for myself.
I cut out 2” square blocks about 1 inch thick and
drilled a 1 1/8” hole through the middle.
I turned a 1 1/8”plug with a 1/4” lip to easily mark
out the napkin outside diameter.
I turned a bushing set to fit on my Pen Mandrel,
consisting of a 1 1/8” diameter spigot and a corresponding sized socket. The 2 inch Holly wood block
slipped on to the spigot and the socket slid up on
the other side of the block. The Holly wood block
was pinched by the sliding tail stock live center.
Nicely gripped on the Pen mandrel, the holly wood
block could be turned round, shaped, sanded and
buffed/waxed.
Displaying in a bowl was a matter of looking for
what was on hand. The napkin rings fitted into a
nice pattern in the bowl, creating the image of
rings with in rings.
The bowl is maple, dyed with Alkaline water based
dye. The inside is red and the rim is a deep purple.
Sprayed with a water based lacquer.
This Month’s Cover PhotoBy Dan Lemire
Napkin rings turned from green Holly wood displayed in a red stained maple bowl.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
Tech TalkBy Bruce Campbell
It seems to have become a habit that we have a
well-attended and spirited Tech Talk every time.
This month there were over thirty participants that
stuck around for nearly 3 hours and, as always, the
topics were wide-ranging and interesting. The online format has provided so many benefits including:
 Open to more participants including Remote
members
 No conflict with other meeting activities
 Time for in-depth discussions
With these major benefits we are likely to keep this
on-line format permanently.
Homemade Hand Wheels
Sheila has purchased a lathe and asked me about
making a hand wheel for it. It is great to have a
hand wheel, especially a wooden one. However,
some guidelines are in order:
Don’t make it too big or too small. If it is too small
it can be hard to get sufficient grip or torque and if
it is too big the higher feed rate can cause excessive friction (think friction burns). Something from
3” to 6” is a good size.
Make your hand wheel with a solid piece of wood
without cracks or knots, sand it very smooth (400
grit+), and apply a durable finish that you can sand
to a non-sticky surface. An imperfect or grabby
surface can be extra dangerous when it is spinning
a several hundred RPMs.
Shape the rim to a bead that fits comfortably in
your hand and is off-center towards the outside of
the wheel. This will make it easier to keep your
hand clear from obstructions.
Check the controls on the outside of the headstock
for anything that sticks out. This can include spindle locks, index pins, or even mounting nuts. Design your wheel to minimize any possible “pinch
points”.
A handy way to
attach
your
hand
wheel
is
with
a
chuck adapter of the
size you need. You
can turn a recess to
accept the adapter
and then glue/screw
it in place. Alternately you can purchase a thread tap
that matches the spindle on your lathe. With it you
can tap the hand wheel so it can simply thread on
to your spindle. The tap is also useful for
mounting other things like waste blocks. But, be
sure to check carefully before buying a tap. Some
lathes have left-handed threads on the outboard
end of the spindle and some also have different
sized threads than the inboard side. Be sure to buy
the right tap.
Finally, the new Laguna Revo 12/16 (a very nice
benchtop lathe, BTW) has a small, metal hand
wheel that also serves to lock the spindle bearing
in place. If you replace it with a hand-made one be
sure to account for this.
Dust Collectors
I have been spending a lot of time turning on my
benchtop lathe and decided it needed a better dust
collection setup. I purchased the Oneida Dust Deputy Deluxe from Lee Valley ($140) to go along with
my shop vac. The Dust Deputy is a small cyclonic
separator that allows very little to get sucked in to
the vacuum cleaner filter bag. Instead it drops in
to the attached bucket.
On the pickup end I attached the upholsterer head

from the shop vac to
the hose and held it in

I do not usually try to
pick up chips when I
turn. I sweep them up,
bag them, and give
them
to
gardening
friends. However, because this small cyclonic separator keeps
the chips out of the
dust bag and makes it easy to empty them in to my

cleaning up. The only downside, of course, is that

My show-and-tell touched off a storm of dust collector solutions that were nothing short of fantastic. Bill showed us his space-safer setup that works
for his small shop.
Next, Don showed us his very interesting “hack”
where he took apart his commercial system,
mounted the motor/impeller unit to the wall and
replumbed it into a cyclonic separator. The barrel is
on a wheeled platform that he lifts to create a seal
and drops to empty. He reports almost never having to clean out the plastic bag shown in the picture below.
Similar systems of this size often are more than 9
feet tall making it difficult to put them in a room
with a standard 8 foot ceiling.
The dust collecting talk continued with Bob showing his “hack”. Like Don, Bob disassembled a storebought unit and placed it impeller unit on a barrel
and ran his collection hoses into the barrel rather
than the impellor. This creates a cyclonic effect
causing the chips and dust to drop out into the barrel. He also reports that the filter bag on the
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)

Bill’s Rikon Portable Dust Collector

Page 7
outflow side rarely has any chips or dust in it.
These are wonderful hacks,
guys. Now I have to take a
closer look at my setup.
Blast Gates and efficiency
loss
Gary asked if there is significant efficiency loss when
adding blast gates into a dust
collection system. Steve reported that he replaced all
the plastic gates with metal
ones in an industrial shop he
runs with a significant improvement in efficiency (and
three to four times the cost).
I shared a hack that clipping
about ¾” off the back corners of the housing of plastic
gates prevents dust from getting stuck in the corners and keeping the gate from closing all the way.
I also apply duct or underlayment tape around the
edges of the body. It helps to reduce leaks in my
system.
Collecting Chips with a Dust Collector
Dan was curious to know how many turners try to
capture chips in their dust collection systems while
they are turning. Most people do not. Most report
that they reserve the dust collector for when they
are sanding and sweep up the chips by hand.
Buffing Abrasives
Bill asked to what grit the various buffing compounds in the Beall system rated? I did some
Googling only to realize that it is not an easy question, mainly because manufacturers seem to have
their own systems.
The Beall and Oneway systems both offer Tripoli as
the “coarsest” grit on their stiffer wheel followed
by White Diamond on a softer wheel and finally
Carnauba on a flannel-like wheel. The “grit” of the
abrasives in not mentioned; just that Tripoli is
coarsest, White Diamond next, and Carnuba rated
as the finest.
I asked how many use carnauba on their work and
a number reported that they do. I found that car-
(Continued from page 6)
(Continued on page 8)
Don Gamble Dust Collector
Bob's Dust
Collector
Beall Buffing System

February 2022
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
nauba “spots” when it comes in contact with water, wet hands, rain drops, etc. Objects that are
not going to be handled might benefit from the
high polish of carnuba but things that will be handled a lot like pens, bottle stoppers, salad bowl,
etc. are not such good candidates.
ShellaWax over CA glue
Dave asked if ShellaWax can be applied over a CAbased finish. A number of people reported good
success with the product when applied over CA
glue.
CA Glue Spreader
I shared a trick that I discovered when applying
CA glue. I use the shiny
closed-cell foam packaging that is used in heavier
items like TVs, or household appliances as a glue
spreader. I cut a block
about 1” square by 2-3”
long and hold it to the
sanded piece while it is turning. I then drop thin CA
glue on the piece while it is turning and wipe the
spreader from side to side. I repeat the application
until the whole surface of the object is covered and
then wipe it down quickly with a shop towel. This
works well for me on objects up to about 3” in diameter.
After 10 or 15 uses a layer of dried CA glue will
build up on the end of the applicator. When this
happens I cut a short piece off with a shop knife
and start again.
Warning: Do NOT use Styrofoam! The CA glue
melts it and makes a mess.
Wall Thickness of Green Bowls
Gary asked what thickness to turn a wet wood
bowl to ensure you will have a round once it dries.
He has tried the 10% rule - leaving the wall thickness 10% of the diameter of the piece – but has not
always had success.
The 10% rule is more a “guide” than a rule. Different species warp more than others and wood harvested from different parts of a tree will warp
more than others. For example, I use 15% when
roughing Oak bowls and find that branch wood
moves more than trunk wood.
But, there is a way to rescue blanks that have
warped too far to get a round. Just boil the blanks
for about 30 minutes in water and it will return to
round. You can re-dry it and it will not warp as
much, or you can green turn it and “Embrace the
Warpage”.
Resin-based Wood Stabilizer
Gary reports that he has recently had success stabilizing punky wood using epoxy resin thinned with
acetone. He paints the mixture on with a brush
applying several coats and it hardens the wood noticeably.
Merv uses lacquer thinned 1:3 with lacquer thinner
for the same job and is also happy with his results.
I bought a can of Minwax Wood Hardener from the
hardware store and found it penetrated well and
did the job I needed.
John has had good success with a product called
Git Rot; a product used in boat maintenance.
Catalyzed Fiberglass Resin
Steve was curious to try catalyzed resin in a turning to
see how it compared with
two part epoxies. Fiberglass
resin itself has no fiber or
glass in it, but is engineered
specifically for laminating
fiberglass cloth and adhering
to wood. The product he
used is a polyester resin: P16 made by Fiberlay. The
resin is activated with a catalyst at one part catalyst to 100 parts resin.
Unlike epoxies he has used, this product mixed
more easily and was far more viscous. The resin
changed from a light translucent blue to light translucent amber... and stayed that way after it set.
The inherent colour of this type of resin can be
problematic for people that either want to control
the colour or want a clear casting.
Bruce added that renowned woodturner Marylin
(Continued from page 7)

Campbell (https://marilyncampbell.ca) has used
epoxies and resins extensively in woodturning and
shared a number of her techniques with us in her
last two visits including how to mix fillers and oilbased paint with resins to create wonderful effects.
See

Soft Edges
Steve shared a good tool tip about softening
square corners on tools. Square edges on the
shafts of flat tool such as skews, and scrapers will
dig in to the toolrest, especially when the turning is
rough. Taking a few minutes to round over those
corners with coarse sandpaper and then polish
them with fine sandpaper will make them slide
over the toolrest more easily and will reduce nicks
and scratches on the toolrest. This is simple to do,
only needs to be done once, and will pay benefits
for the like of the tool.
Angle of Edge on a Skew
Pippa was gifted a skew with a very flat cutting
edge. She loved the quality of the cuts but had to
tip the tool well over to get the tool to make a
skewing cut. Her question was to what angle
should the tool be ground so it will be easier to
use?
There was lots of advice given over this but it all
boiled down to about a 45 degree angle with the
two bevels nearly the same, meeting near the center of the tool and “not too long”. The longer the
bevel is on a tool the harder it is to control so start
by grinding them about as long as the skew is thick
and make them longer as you gain more experience.
Here is a page from a 2003 Focus on Fundamentals
handout on the skew.
Crepe sandpaper cleaner
Dan does a fair amount of green turning and that
involves lots of wet sanding. He discovered that he
can clean his sandpaper quickly by running it over a
crepe block. It is so successful that he made a permanent holder for the block located close to where
he works.
Thanks for sharing, Dan.
Compressor Muffler
Finally, Brian has recently installed a new compressor outside his shop. Unfortunately, it makes a LOT
of racket so he decided to put “mufflers” on the
system. Here is his story:
Contrary to my expectations, I discovered that the
most of the offensive noise from my new (to me)
compressor is from the intake of air. I decided I
needed to beef up the mufflers on the three piston
heads.
(Continued from page 8)
(Continued on page 10)

February 2022
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
I removed the mufflers and attached 90* elbows
and attached a length of heavy duty garden hose to
the elbow and then clamped the mufflers on the
other end.
This allowed me to stick the mufflers into a 5 gallon
bucket lined with foam to see if it would dampen
the sound. I was able to reduce the sound from
95dB (very loud) to 75dB (heavy traffic).
My next step will be to build foam lined housing
with a staggered air inlet and outlet with a fan pulling air through the housing.
This should further reduce the compressor noise so
that neighbours can have a beer in their back yard
and not be annoyed that my compressor is running.
I sure the neighbours appreciate your efforts, Brian, and maybe you will get invited over now for
one of those beverages.
As you can see, we covered a lot of topics last time.
Thanks to all for you that participated. Please plan
to join us next time – 7:00PM Monday Feb 28th,
2022 via ZOOM. As usual, you will get an email
with the ZOOM credentials.

Feb 2022 Meeting Demonstration: 3
-Cornerd Boxes
By Bruce Campbell
I had a great deal of fun meeting the August 2021
President’s Challenge “Repurposed”. It inspired
me to make a 3-conered box (see https://gvwg.ca/
docs/Newsletter2021/September2021.pdf
pg21).
That effort inspired me to make 10 more similar
boxes for an annual exhibition at Place des Arts in
Port Coquitlam called Positively Petite. Each box
became a canvas on which I could explore a number of the surface decoration techniques I have
seen over the years. That included pyrography,
sand blasting, texturing, masking/painting, piercing, mixed media, and so on.
In the main demonstration for our February
meeting I will go through the (quite simple) setup,
tools, and techniques for making a 3-cornered box
and then discuss some design choices and surface
enhancement technique that can add interest to
them and allow for hundreds of different results.

The World of ResinsBy Gary Burns
It was a simple case of turning a spalted piece of
wood. Anyone turning badly spalted wood will
know you end up with tear out. Mother nature is
claiming the wood by starting the decay process.
So here lies the challenge, and I do love challenges.
How to make spalted wood usable without tear
out.
Resins to harden wood come in a lot of different
types. Plus, there are so many different concoctions of adding finishing products to different thinners to try to penetrate into the soft wood surface
to harden it. Every one I tried had some success,
usually about 1/4" max for my attempts, but I
wanted deeper penetration. Why? Well, I wanted
to make peppermills from highly soft spalted wood.
I love the colours. I wanted the inside of the peppermill to be rock hard as well.
So not knowing where this world of hardening
deep penetration would take me, off I went. I can’t
list every concoction I have tried or every brand of
hardener I have bought as that would fill a book.
But if you have heard of one, I will bet I tried it.
So, as the dollars kept flying out the door, the frustrations from not getting where I was wanting to go
didn’t make me want to quit. It only made me mad
and more determined.
All this searching and experimenting lead me to a
product called Cactus Juice by Turntex in the USA.
And what a journey this became! The product did
what I was after, but it was just not a paint on
product. This product required a vacuum pump, a
vacuum chamber, and a toaster oven for small
stuff. However, my peppermills don't fit a toaster
oven so this required the wife to go shopping so I
could use a full-size oven to bake the resin impregnated wood.
I was learning my stubbornness was coming at a
cost. (by sending her shopping ha ha)
So, since this is an expensive product, I found I was
further ahead to rough turn my items oversize,
with lots of tear out still there, then go through the
process. Put the rough turned item in a vacuum
chamber, weigh it down so its not floating, fill past
the top with cactus juice (which I later discovered
is dyable, cool). Turn on the pump and suck out all
the air, tons of air, sometimes days running the
pump. When no more air comes out of the wood,
turn off the pump. The wood acts like a sponge,
sucking the juice back into itself. Leave everything
for a few days soaking. The Cactus juice does not
harden by itself, it requires heat. Finally take the
piece or pieces out and bake them.
Mission accomplished. A totally rotten spalted
piece of wood that is hard as a rock,
It turns beautifully, with zero tear out, but don’t
expect long shavings. It also sands wonderfully.
Turning hard woods would have been easier but
spalted has colours not in hardwoods.
And remember it was a challenge...
Was it worth the cost and a two-year journey?
Very likely not, but a challenge I wanted to find the
answer to. Plus, it opened up a whole new world of
resins that now lead me into making hybrids; hardened wood and other brands of resins combined
into one piece. That’s another story, another day
with pressure pots, moulds etc.

for Covid Clearance, Youtube offers a plethora of

too many are not good or are unsafe. Some are
outrageously scary. Here are some very good videos/channels/people to look toward for quality
turning tips with generally safe practices (see note

Tip: Because these turners might have differing approaches to the same tool it is wise to stick with
ONE teacher until you have mastered that particular skill.
Note: Even the well-seasoned pros and those that
should know better will make little mistakes
around the lathe. You will notice all of the above
break some these safety rules some times:
•
Using one’s hand to slow down a turning blank
•
Moving the tool rest while the lathe is running
•
One-handed operation of a gouge(or any tool)
•
Spinning a blank onto a screw chuck WHILE the
lathe is running

Practice and PlayBy Sheila Balzer, WIT Liaison
As I made the submission
to the January 2022 Instant
Gallery I was reflecting and
realizing all the people who
have been influential for
playing with the tools, techniques, materials, and support which resulting in the
creation of this tiny piece
of creative play. This shawl
pin has since been sent off
to with the shawl to Gwenda’s high school friend
who lives in Valley City in Ohio.
The embellishments were inspired by Joanne
Sauvageau who had a demo using Pebeo Prisme
paints. Her completed platter piece was featured
on the cover of WOW magazine.
Barbara
Dill –
Multi
axis
turning
https://
virtualwoodturningdemos.com/barbara-dill/
Although the twig was only turned once on the
same axis, I had to employ techniques demonstrated by Barbara, especially light cuts and being mindful of the shadows and spaces.
Dr. Seri Robinson – spalted wood https://
www.northernspalting.com/about-us/dr-spalting/
There is spalting on this boxwood. First with
WWOS 2020, then again as a GVWG IRD, Seri
opened a whole new world of appreciating wood
and fungi.
Cindy Drozda – taking new turners through the
basic in very enlightening ways. Her up close camera work and very thorough explanations made a
huge difference on getting the more confident with
the
basics
and
the
possibilities.
http://
www.cindydrozda.com/html/teaching.html
All the participants of the 2021 WIT Virtual Exchange especially Linda Ferber, Marie Anderson,
Cheryl Lewis, Barbara Silberman, Kathleen Duncan
and Andi Wolfe who led by example, inspire or
were my teammates during the exchange.
The stick used for this pin was first turned for a
possible project as part of our WIT team submission but was not incorporated so it sat for the next
opportunity of inspiration, learning and play.
Plus, Joey Richardson, Barbara Dill, Andi Wolfe, Sally Burnett, Dixie Biggs, Kristin LeVier, Merryll
Saylan, Donna Zils, Kimberly Winkle, Betty
Scarpino, Beth Ireland, Kailee Bocsh, Rebecca

tab. As a new turner, if you are looking for inspiration of the process of others, be sure to check out
this amazing resource.
There is so much appreciation and gratitude to all
the individuals who have been part of my
woodturning journey so far. All the time, attention, conversations, tips, support, and details each
have shared as I have had the wonderful opportunity to explore this and other simple pieces of
play. (In no particular order, mostly. Keep in mind,
there are only a handful of people on this list that I
knew prior to August 2020, when my woodturning
journey began.)
Since starting this month’s submission and the list
above, there are a whole bunch more turners and
artists both within our Guild and the awesome
presentations by a wide variety of turners through
the WWOS, Meet the Turner, and Instagram and
Facebook Live demos.
While finishing this article, The Tiny Turner, Emma
Cook was completing her Gonk-a-thon: Part Deux.

(she turned bodies well past 1 am the night before). This was a great example of repetitive tool

Magnetic Dust Collection Connectors By via John Hammond
Inspired by a YouTube video.
One of my biggest problems with dust collection
systems is that they cost a lot, and they are inconvenient to use. This means for a quick job they
don’t get used. Most jobs in our shops are quick
jobs. Trimming a piece of wood to fit, a quick touch
to a sander to get rid of a pencil line or round a corner, we all do it.
To fix the problem we buy waste gates and tubing
and clamps and special switches to turn on dust
collectors remotely and fittings to hang tubing on
the wall, all at a high cost. I’m cheap, and my
grandparents would haunt me if I threw money
away like that - so here is a small piece of that puzzle.
With a magnetic fitting I can move a hose quickly
and easily from machine to machine. In my small
shop I don’t have room to mount hose every which
way - so I have one hose from my dust collector
(outside) in to my shop. On the end I have a magnetic coupler that mates with another coupler on
the band saw and another on the table saw (two of
the best dust makers in my shop). With a quick
twist I can move from one to another very easily.
I hope the diagrams below have enough information for you to build your own system. This is for
a 4 inch hose; you will have to adjust for your size
needs.

My source of information is: - YouTube - Magnet
dust port adapters by the Ring Workshop. There
are other interesting ideas on this video as to
where to put the hoses (no, no let’s keep it clean
now).
This is the list of ingredients, and layout of the
holes. The magnets cannot bang onto each other
‘cause they are very brittle and will break, so the
holes must be deep enough for 2 magnets and
glue, keeping the surface of the magnet just below
the surface of the plywood. Also the polarity of the
magnets is important so pay close attention to the
little red dot on the magnets. The red dot attracts
to the side without a red dot. If you make a mistake on this part you will have to start again.

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 41)

February 2022
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 41
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
